implementation_notes: Ruby's standard library has threads and Queue but no futures, so the aggregator is hand-written: fan-out threads push partial messages onto a Queue (or into a Mutex-guarded Hash keyed by correlation id) and the collecting thread loops with Queue#pop(timeout:) until the expected count or the deadline is reached, then merges and publishes; every collector loop therefore needs an explicit deadline and every shared structure a mutex. The concurrent-ruby gem offers Concurrent::Promises.zip/all? as a library alternative when futures semantics are enough, but the classic collector remains the right shape when partials arrive from outside the process and must be keyed, de-duplicated and expired.
code_sketch:
results = Queue.new
vendors.each { |v| Thread.new { results << ask(v) } }
quotes = []
while quotes.size < vendors.size
  q = results.pop(timeout: 5) or break   # time-out completeness condition
  quotes << q
end
best = quotes.min_by(&:rate)             # aggregation algorithm
publish(best)
pitfalls: The GVL means CPU-bound partials do not run in parallel: threads only buy latency for I/O-bound asks, while Ractors or processes are needed for CPU parallelism.
Queue#pop without a timeout (or a Hash without a Mutex) blocks forever or corrupts state when a partial never arrives - every collector loop needs a deadline and synchronized state.
Exceptions raised inside a Thread die silently unless the thread is joined and Thread.abort_on_exception is set, so a failed partial is indistinguishable from a slow one.
